title: Secret Cold War Projects That Were Actually Real
title_candidates: Secret Cold War Projects That Were Actually Real
The CIA Stole a Soviet Submarine (And 3 More Real Cold War Secrets)
4 Cold War Secrets That Sound Fake But Are Real
blurb: Meatball investigates four secret Cold War projects that were real: Operation Popeye (the US tried to make it rain on the Ho Chi Minh Trail), Project A119 (a plan to set off a nuclear bomb on the Moon), Project Iceworm (nuclear missiles under the Greenland ice) and Project Azorian (the CIA's fake mining ship that tried to steal a sunken Soviet submarine). Every claim comes from public records; sources are in the description.

beats.say: In nineteen seventy-four, the CIA built a giant ship to steal a Soviet submarine. From three miles under the Pacific. And it told the world the ship was mining rocks.
Four secret Cold War projects. All actually real. Counting down to number one, the submarine heist. That one's at the end.

beats.say: And honestly? I'm nervous. If the government can hide a whole ship, it can definitely hide one meatball. In a sandwich.
Comment your guess before I tell you. Which one cost the most? The rain machine? The moon bomb? The ice city? Or the submarine heist? Lock it in.
I'm Meatball. I open the files nobody was supposed to read. Subscribe. A new case every Tuesday and Saturday.
Number four. Vietnam, nineteen sixty-seven. Trucks keep moving supplies down a jungle road network called the Ho Chi Minh Trail.
Bombing it isn't stopping them. So somebody asks a strange question. What if we just made it rain more?

shots.photo: Map of the Ho Chi Minh Trail

beats.say: That's Operation Popeye. Planes flew over the trail and fired flares full of silver iodide into the clouds. It's called cloud seeding.
The goal: more rain, more mud, washed-out roads and landslides. A longer rainy season, made to order.
As a meatball, I take this personally. Rain plus dirt is exactly how you ruin a meatball. This is a weapon against me.
The crews even had a motto. Make mud, not war.
Here's the twist. It ran in secret for five years, until reporters broke the story in nineteen seventy-one and seventy-two.

shots.photo: Map of the Ho Chi Minh Trail

beats.say: Did it work? The military thought it stretched the rainy season a little. Scientists still argue. But the world agreed on one thing.
In nineteen seventy-seven, countries signed a treaty banning weather as a weapon. It's called ENMOD. Weather wars: officially banned.
So the US tried to control the rain. Number three aimed higher. It wanted to blow up something on the Moon.
Number three. Nineteen fifty-eight. The Soviets have just launched Sputnik, and America is panicking.
beats.chapter: Project A119: the plan to nuke the Moon

beats.say: So the Air Force quietly asks scientists in Chicago. Could we set off a nuclear bomb on the Moon?
Not to destroy it. To show off. A flash so big that people on Earth could see it. Basically the most expensive selfie ever.
The report was called A Study of Lunar Research Flights. The project's name: A119.
One of the young scientists doing the math was Carl Sagan. His job: work out how the dust cloud would spread.
I'd like to point out that the Moon looks a lot like a giant meatball. So yes. I'm taking this one personally too.
Here's the catch. They never did it. One worry: if the rocket failed, the bomb could come back down on Earth.
It stayed secret for about forty years, until the project's leader, Leonard Reiffel, talked about it in two thousand.
If you didn't know the Moon nearly got nuked, hit like. It helps me open more files.
That one stayed on paper. Number two didn't. They actually built it. Inside the ice.
Number two. Greenland, nineteen fifty-nine. The US Army starts building a town inside the ice sheet. It's called Camp Century.
beats.chapter: Project Iceworm: missiles under the ice

beats.say: Tunnels cut into the ice, with buildings inside them. Labs, a chapel, a barber shop. And its own nuclear reactor.

shots.photo: Camp Century's PM-2A portable nuclear reactor (US Army)

beats.say: The public story was a science base, studying the ice. And they really did study the ice.
But here's the secret part. The Army had a plan called Project Iceworm. Thousands of kilometers of tunnels, hiding about six hundred nuclear missiles under the ice.
Close enough to reach the Soviet Union. And Denmark, which Greenland belongs to, wasn't told about the missile plan.
I'd last about four seconds in there. Meatballs freeze. Then you're not a meatball, you're a hockey puck.
Then the ice fought back. Ice sheets move. The tunnels kept squeezing shut, and crews had to keep shaving the walls back.
By nineteen sixty-seven, Camp Century was abandoned. The missiles never came. The plan only came out in the nineteen nineties, through Danish research.
And the camp is still down there, frozen, with its waste. Scientists warn melting ice could uncover it by the end of this century.
Three cases down. Number one, the one I promised you, the submarine heist. And it starts with a billionaire.
Number one. March, nineteen sixty-eight. A Soviet submarine called K-129 sinks in the Pacific, with ninety-eight men on board.
beats.chapter: Project Azorian: the CIA's submarine heist

beats.say: The Soviets search and can't find it. The US can. It's lying about three miles down, with nuclear missiles inside, and maybe secret codes.
So the CIA decides to steal it. Nobody had ever lifted anything that big from that deep. They need a giant ship with a giant claw.

shots.photo: CIA painting of the AZORIAN recovery

beats.say: And they need a reason for that ship to exist. Enter Howard Hughes, one of the richest men in the world.
He lends his name to the cover story: a ship to mine the ocean floor for metal lumps called manganese nodules.

shots.photo: Manganese nodule from the cover story (CIA)

beats.say: The ship is called the Hughes Glomar Explorer. Magazines loved it. It was all a cover.
I respect this. I've been pretending to be a normal meatball for years. Nobody suspects a thing.
Summer, nineteen seventy-four. A Soviet ship sails up and watches. The crew keeps a straight face. Just mining rocks. Nothing to see here.
The claw goes down on miles of steel pipe. It grabs the submarine. And slowly, it starts to lift.

shots.photo: CIA model of the sunken K-129

beats.say: Then, here's the twist. On the way up, part of the claw breaks. Most of the submarine falls back into the deep.

shots.photo: CIA painting of the AZORIAN recovery

beats.say: They bring up one piece. Inside are the remains of six Soviet sailors.

shots.photo: CIA model of the sunken K-129

beats.say: No joke here. The crew buried them at sea, with a Soviet flag and a funeral service, and filmed it. Years later, the US gave Russia that film.
In nineteen seventy-five, the story leaked to the newspapers. A reporter asked the CIA about it, and got an answer that's now famous.
We can neither confirm nor deny. That sentence is called the Glomar response, after this ship. Spy agencies still use it today.
A rain weapon, a moon bomb, an ice town, a fake mining ship. All four, real.
And the one that cost the most, by far? The submarine heist. Hundreds of millions of dollars, in nineteen seventies money.
